Mazamet is a commune in the Tarn department of Occitanie, southern France, at the northern foot of the Montagne Noire. The town developed below the medieval stronghold of Hautpoul, overlooking the valley of the Arnette.

A centre of woollen manufacture, Mazamet became internationally prominent in the nineteenth century through délainage, the separation of wool from sheepskins. Its factories processed skins imported from several continents, and the wealth of the wool trade financed substantial houses and commercial buildings.

Mazamet is also associated with the Sirven affair, in which Voltaire campaigned to overturn the conviction of a Protestant family, and with Mazamet, ville morte, a televised road-safety demonstration staged by its inhabitants in 1973.
Geography and natural environment

Mazamet lies where the Arnette descends from the Montagne Noire towards the Thoré. The river runs through the town before joining the Thoré at its north-eastern boundary. The steep valley above the town became a corridor of industrial development, with factories taking advantage of the river's water.

The surrounding Haut-Languedoc landscape lies at the meeting of Atlantic, Mediterranean and mountain climatic influences. Across the regional natural park, these differences sustain contrasting habitats: beech woods and conifer forests on higher ground, oak and chestnut woodland on valley slopes, and evergreen oak woodland in Mediterranean sectors.
Streams, rocky slopes, clearings and mature trees contribute to the park's biodiversity.
History
Hautpoul and the medieval town

Mazamet's early history is linked to Hautpoul, a fortified settlement on a rocky ridge above the Arnette valley. During the Albigensian Crusade, Simon de Montfort besieged Hautpoul in 1212. The siege and subsequent movement of inhabitants towards the valley form part of the history of Mazamet's development.

A thirteenth-century charter issued by Jourdain de Saissac, lord of Hautpoul, granted privileges to the inhabitants of Hautpoul and the settlement beside the Arnette. The name Mas Arnette has been proposed as the origin of Mazamet, although alternative explanations exist.
The name Mazamet is documented in the fifteenth century, by 1462, the settlement had fortifications and an enclosing wall.
Reformation and religious conflict

Mazamet became a Protestant stronghold during the French Wars of Religion. Its position in the Montagne Noire made it a resource base for Protestant forces. A period of respite under Henry IV was followed by renewed warfare under Louis XIII, when the forces of the Prince of Condé devastated the town.
Religious divisions continued to shape its social and political history long after the fighting.
The Sirven affair and Voltaire

In the eighteenth century, a prosecution near Mazamet became one of Voltaire's campaigns against religious intolerance. The Protestant surveyor Pierre-Paul Sirven lived at Saint-Alby with his wife and three daughters. His daughter Élisabeth, who experienced serious mental-health difficulties, was placed in a Catholic convent in 1760 before being returned to her family.

The family was accused of killing her. Sirven and his wife were sentenced to death in their absence, their property was confiscated, and their effigies were publicly burned in Mazamet in 1764. They fled to Switzerland and sought Voltaire's assistance.

Voltaire publicised their case and helped mobilise support across Europe. Sirven returned to France and surrendered to the authorities in Mazamet in August 1769. In November 1771, the criminal chamber at Toulouse overturned the earlier sentence and restored his property.
The affair brought a local prosecution into the wider Enlightenment debate over religious persecution and justice.
Wool, sheepskins and international trade

In 1851, industrialist Pierre-Élie Houlès imported raw sheepskins from Argentina and experimented with recovering their wool. The resulting process, known as délainage, allowed both wool and leather to be used rather than sacrificing one to obtain the other.

The soft, low-lime water of the Arnette was particularly suited to the process, which used fermentation to loosen the wool. From the 1870s, Mazamet firms established purchasing offices in producing countries, selling the recovered wool to textile manufacturers and the stripped skins to leather processors.
The textile crisis of the 1880s encouraged factories to convert to the more profitable activity.

Supply networks reached Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and North Africa, buyers included European, American and Russian markets. In the record year of 1912, more than 32 million sheepskins were processed at Mazamet. The industry linked the town's narrow river valley to livestock production and manufacturing across the world.

Industrial wealth was accompanied by arduous, poorly paid work. Some labourers combined factory employment with farming, and employers later recruited workers from abroad. Competition and changes in demand eventually undermined the industry, whose decline accelerated in the later twentieth century.
Labour politics and the strike of 1909

Mazamet's industrial society had an unusual political pattern. As historian Maurice Agulhon observed in his review of Rémy Cazals's study of the town, its largely Catholic working class could be more conservative than its predominantly Protestant employers. Many workers supported opponents of the Republic, yet also took part in determined trade-union action.

In 1909, workers in the sheepskin-processing industry conducted a four-month strike. Troops were deployed in the area, while the strikers received support from the CGT, including Victor Griffuelhes, and from Jean Jaurès. The dispute ended in a workers' victory. Cazals reconstructed it from union and company archives, police reports, newspapers and oral testimony.
Resistance and liberation

During the Second World War, Resistance groups in the Montagne Noire and the Sidobre took part in operations around Mazamet. On 22 August 1944, a German column approaching from Carcassonne encountered Resistance fighters in the town.

According to the account of former members of the Corps franc du Sidobre reported by La Dépêche du Midi, the Resistance moved an old tank through the streets to give the impression of greater strength. After exchanges of fire and negotiations, 385 German officers and soldiers surrendered at the Stade de la Chevalière.
Mazamet, ville morte
On 17 May 1973, Mazamet became the setting for a national road-safety campaign. Its population of about 16,600 was comparable to the number of people killed on French roads in the preceding year.
Residents were asked to lie down outside their homes and workplaces, turning the streets into a representation of an entire town killed in road accidents.

Conceived by journalist Michel Tauriac and filmed by director Guy Seligmann, the operation lasted about ten minutes. The resulting television programme, Mazamet, la ville rayée de la carte, used the town to make the scale of road deaths visible.
The campaign took place in the same year that France introduced major measures on seat belts, motorcycle helmets and speed limits.
Economy and commercial renewal

Following the decline of the wool-processing industry, Mazamet's economy diversified into food production, pharmaceutical activities, dental supplies, metal construction and services. Businesses identified by the municipality include Menguy's, Laboratoires Pierre Fabre, SOFIC and Cabrol Construction Métallique.
Commercial activity expanded during the 2010s and early 2020s. In October 2025, La Dépêche du Midi reported that the town had recorded 183 shop openings and 86 closures since 2014.

In September 2024, then-mayor Olivier Fabre stated that almost all commercial units in the central shopping area were occupied, as the municipality extended its scheme supporting the establishment or takeover of local shops.

INSEE recorded 148 business creations in the commune in 2025, compared with 82 in 2015, in the non-agricultural market economy. 4 per cent were individual enterprises. These figures measure new registrations rather than net increases in the number of businesses.
The census recorded 4,608 jobs located in the commune in 2023, compared with 4,774 in 2017.

Industrial investment has continued alongside this commercial renewal. Menguy's, established in Mazamet since 1987, announced a second production facility in 2025. The municipality described the project as retaining 170 existing jobs and adding 40 positions by completion, including ten already created during the project's development. The proposed plant includes production lines for peanut butter.

The municipality introduced a first-year rent-support scheme for new or transferred town-centre shops in 2018. The assistance was calculated at €5 per square metre per month, capped at €250 monthly, or €3,000 annually.
